title: Ashvaghosha himself
hook: a brahmin-born poet and monk, remembered also for the poem of Nanda

segments.voice: Yesterday: final nirvana, and the poem's ending kept in Tibetan and Chinese. Your line, the poem traveled. Today, the person who wrote it.

For weeks now, there's been a voice behind every scene. The king's fear in the palace. The worms in the plowed field. The gates swinging open without a sound. Mara's flowers. The long night under the tree. Someone chose every one of those pictures, and the words to hold them. His name is Ashvaghosha. And here's the honest part: we know very little about him. We have a short signature at the end of his poems, a handful of later stories, and the poems themselves.
screen: `A VOICE BEHIND EVERY SCENE.` → `HIS NAME: ASHVAGHOSHA.` → `WE KNOW VERY LITTLE.`

segments.voice: First, the signature. At the close of his other long poem, the author names himself: Ashvaghosha of Saketa, son of a woman named Suvarnakshi, a monk, a great poet and speaker. His town, his mother's name, and that he wore the robe. Not much more. Second, the brahmin. Later tradition says he was born a brahmin and trained in the old learning before he became a follower of the Buddha. His poems seem to agree. They are full of the old kings, sages and heroes of the Indian epics, used the way a well-read writer drops in names a learned audience will know. He doesn't throw that learning away. He puts it to work. Third, the poem of Nanda. His other surviving poem tells of Nanda, the Buddha's half-brother, newly married to a beautiful wife, Sundari, and deeply in love. The Buddha brings him into the order, and Nanda is miserable, thinking only of her. The poem follows him patiently, through longing, through a strange journey to see heavenly women, and on, step by step, until he lets go of craving altogether and finds peace. It's a poem about someone who did not want to be a monk, and how he got there anyway. Fourth, the monk who wrote. Put the pieces together and you get an unusual figure: a monk who lived by a discipline of simplicity, and who also wrote richly ornate verse. He didn't see those as opposites. A poet monk. Tomorrow, in his own words, why.
screen: `A SIGNATURE: SAKETA, SUVARNAKSHI.` · `BORN A BRAHMIN, TRADITION SAYS.` · `THE POEM OF NANDA.` · `SIMPLE ROBE, RICH VERSE.` · then, large: `A POET MONK.`

segments.voice: Choose one verse you love, a line from a sacred text, a poem from school, or one of these weeks' scenes in your own words, and say it aloud, slowly, once. Listen to how it sounds in the room, then sit with the quiet that follows.
Ashvaghosha himself. A monk from Saketa, brahmin-born, tradition says, who wrote the life of the Buddha and the poem of Nanda in verse. Today's word.
Your line: a poet monk. A simple robe and rich verse, with no quarrel between them. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Ashvaghosha's poems are read today in Sanskrit classes and in translation by students of Buddhism and of Indian literature, and the story of Nanda is retold in Buddhist teaching about craving and letting go.

chat.says: Do we know much about the man who wrote that poem on the Buddha's life?
options: Very little: a short signature, a few later stories, and the poems.
Yes, a full biography of him survives, written by his students.
Nothing at all; nobody even knows the poet's name.
chat.meaning: His signature names Saketa, his mother Suvarnakshi, and his robe. Beyond that we have later stories and the poems themselves.

notes: Colophon: confirm that the Saundarananda colophon names Ashvaghosha as of Saketa, son of Suvarnakshi, a bhikshu, and calls him a great poet and great speaker (mahakavi, mahavadin). The script states nothing else from it.
Brahmin birth: from later tradition (e.g. the Chinese life attributed to Kumarajiva); framed as 'later tradition says'.
'His poems seem to agree': the claim that the poems are full of epic kings and sages is a characterization; confirm that cantos such as 4 and 9 cite epic figures as examples, and soften if needed.
Confirm the Saundarananda's outline: Nanda and Sundari, reluctant ordination, the journey to see the apsarases, gradual instruction and liberation.
'His other surviving poem' assumes the two complete kavya attributions; other works are attributed to him with less certainty. 'At least one other long poem' in the trapdoor keeps this open.
